articles.title: How has the European Union’s major recovery plan benefited the 27 member states?
articles.summary: The 27 member states of the European Union agreed in July 2020 on a €750 billion post-Covid recovery plan called NextGenerationEU. Its main instrument is the Recovery and Resilience Facility, through which the European Commission has already disbursed €450 billion. The programme is due to come to an end in a few months, and countries must claim and account for the remaining funds.
articles.content:

The Recovery and Resilience Facility provides for negotiated national plans that entitle member states to grants and, in some cases, loans. These funds have amounted to several percentage points of GDP for member states. The main beneficiaries include Italy, Spain, Poland, Portugal, France and Romania.

We turn our attention to a small country at the heart of Europe: Belgium. In Belgium's Francophone community government, for example, 149 school sites have been selected for renovation, including the Athénée royal de Ganshoren. Just a few years ago, its secondary school was so dilapidated that students, parents and teachers protested to demand renovation work. Yet the task remains immense: much of the French-speaking school building stock is still outdated and energy inefficient.

articles.personality_title: How the EU’s Recovery Plan Is Helping Member Countries Rebuild
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In July 2020, the 27 countries of the European Union agreed on a big recovery plan called NextGenerationEU. It was created to help the EU bounce back from the problems caused by the Covid-19 pandemic. The plan includes a fund called the Recovery and Resilience Facility.

**What happened** – Since then, the European Commission has given out €450 billion to the member countries through this fund. Countries use this money to support their economies and improve things like schools and infrastructure. For example, in Belgium’s French-speaking community, 149 schools are being renovated, including one that was in very bad shape before.

**Impact** – This plan is important because it gives each country money based on their needs, helping them fix real problems. It covers a good part of each country’s economy and helps improve everyday places like schools. The work in Belgium shows how the money is making a visible difference for students and teachers.

**What’s next step** – The recovery plan is ending soon, so countries must finish their projects and report on how they used the money. This will help make sure the funds were spent well and could guide future efforts to support the EU’s growth and recovery.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The EU’s NextGenerationEU fund is helping member countries rebuild their economies and improve public services with large investments like school renovations.
articles.personality_title_fr: Comment le plan de relance de l’UE aide les pays membres à se reconstruire

articles.personality_title_es: Cómo el plan de recuperación de la UE está ayudando a los países miembros a reconstruirse

articles.title: What’s the secret sauce for happy scientists at work? These eight countries offer some clues
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03226-5Meaningful work, flexibility and job security all matter more than salaries do, Nature’s job satisfaction survey shows.
articles.content:
Nature’s 2026 job satisfaction survey This article is the first in a series discussing the results of Nature’s 2026 science-job satisfaction survey. It’s the latest edition of such surveys, which started in 2010; the last two took place in 2018 and 2021. The 2026 survey, created in partnership with Thinks Insight & Strategy, a research consultancy in London, launched in May and was advertised on nature.com, in Springer Nature digital products and through e-mail campaigns. It had 3,882 self-selecting respondents across 133 countries with 31% describing themselves as female and 19% as belonging to a minority ethnic group in their country of work. The full survey data sets are available at go.nature.com/4b2drrc.

Scientists might grumble about shrinking grants, mounting paperwork and long hours, but most are happy at work. When Nature’s careers team surveyed almost 4,000 scientists in May and June, 61% reported feeling at least moderately satisfied with their jobs. Around 75% felt either optimistic or neutral about their job prospects, and 65% would recommend a research career to students.

Salary ranked low as a driver of satisfaction, coming seventh out of eight factors assessed. Doing meaningful and engaging work and having a good work–life balance, job security and sufficient research funding, for instance, were all viewed as more important than take-home pay. Late-career scientists, those with permanent positions and those earning more than the equivalent of US$50,000 a year are more satisfied than are other researchers. Men are more optimistic than women: 56% of men feel positive about their career outlook compared with 44% of women (see ‘Nature’s 2026 job satisfaction survey’).

Respondents working in industry were not significantly more satisfied than those in academia — a change since the last survey, in 2021 (see ‘Looking back at scientist satisfaction’). This is despite industry scientists earning 66%, on average, more than do academics, according to the 2026 survey. “This is very interesting and shows that satisfaction is about more than money,” says Henry Sauermann, a science-policy scholar at the European School of Management and Technology in Berlin. Academic scientists probably enjoy other benefits, he notes, such as greater research autonomy than their industry colleagues have and the ability to do interesting work.

Looking back at scientist satisfaction A showcase of Nature’s salary and satisfaction surveys reveals how opinions have shifted over the past 16 years. 2010: For love and money Researchers’ self-reported contentment with their chosen profession depends on more than just salaries. 2012: Turbulent times Many scientists are content with their work, but uneasy about finances. 2014: Divided opinions Financial woes are marring researchers’ enjoyment of their work. 2016: Reality check A feeling that good performance is not adequately rewarded is pervading the research world. 2018: Satisfaction in science The last survey before the COVID-19 pandemic showed that many researchers were happy with their career. 2021: Hurdles to career satisfaction Scientists are concerned about their career prospects because of funding shortages, intense competition for jobs and COVID-19 disruptions.

A lack of funding and too few available jobs are the main barriers to career advancement, the survey found. Respondents were asked which one workplace change would make the most difference to their careers. Answers included mandated work breaks and staff networking sessions — suggested by an academic in Japan, where 22% of respondents were dissatisfied with their relationships with their colleagues. Others suggested raising wages to cover living costs, including an academic in Ethiopia, where 73% of survey respondents say that their salaries don’t cover basic living costs. Working overtime did not seem to affect overall job satisfaction globally, suggesting that long working hours are normalized in many science jobs. But those who worked overtime were less likely to be satisfied with their work–life balance than those who worked only their contracted hours.

Are these the happiest PhD students in the world?

Job satisfaction seems to have mostly bounced back to levels from before the COVID-19 pandemic. In the 2021 survey, 53% of respondents reported that their job satisfaction had worsened over the preceding 12 months. Now, just 33% say it had worsened over the past year and for the largest group of respondents, 39%, it had stayed the same. The proportion of satisfied respondents has increased slightly from 58% in 2021 to 61% this year. But it remains lower than in 2018, when 68% responded feeling satisfied. Shifts in people’s satisfaction differed depending on the country they worked in. Satisfaction of China’s researchers dropped by 24 percentage points since 2018 to 51% this year; in the United States, the drop was only 3 percentage points. Italy is the only country to remain stable at 64%.

Such comparisons should be treated with caution, however, because of shifts in the self-selecting respondents’ locations. This year’s survey drew scientists from 133 countries. The largest share (39%) lived in Asia, followed by Europe (25%) and North and Central America (17%). That is a reversal of 2018, when about 40% of respondents lived in North and Central America, 35% in Europe and 16% in Asia. The mix of career stages and job sectors reported also differ by country.

We took a closer look at some of the nations with at least 100 respondents to dig deeper into what makes scientists happy — or not — in 2026 (see ‘How happy are scientists with their jobs?’).

Oh, Canada!

Canada has the highest overall satisfaction rate (76%) of the ten countries with more than 100 responses. Significantly more scientists than the global average are happy with their opportunities to work on interesting projects (81% versus 60% overall), their level of independence (81% versus 72%), the meaningfulness of their job (80% versus 66%), their ability to work remotely (69% versus 49%), their benefits (66% versus 46%), the inclusivity at their workplace (62% versus 50%) and their salaries (61% versus 44%).

“None of these findings surprise me,” says Glen Jones, a higher-education researcher at the University of Toronto in Canada. Although there are challenges because of growing workloads and researchers having short-term contracts, Jones says that academics — who make up 64% of Canada’s respondents — “generally report a supportive working environment” and “believe that they have high levels of academic freedom and professional autonomy”.

Canada’s government has made large commitments to science funding when other nations are reducing such spending, says David Robinson, executive director of the Canadian Association of University Teachers in Ottawa. He thinks that this bolsters satisfaction, although the high number of people in unions at Canadian universities also has a role. “This translates on average into better job security, decent salaries and benefits,” he says.

Robinson also says that “the anti-science policies of the administration of US President Donald Trump may very well be casting a more positive light on Canada”, potentially boosting satisfaction. Dozens of US scholars have relocated to Canada as part of an international recruitment drive, according to a Canadian government announcement in August. “We’re not without our problems and challenges, but when we look south of the border, researchers may be taking some comfort in knowing they are comparatively faring much better,” he says.

India’s youthful optimism

With 541 respondents, India has the largest sample of any country surveyed. Its scientists were the most optimistic about their career prospects of the ten countries with more than 100 respondents. Despite average numbers of scientists reporting being satisfied (59%), 70% of respondents feel positive about their prospects and 82% would recommend a career in science — both proportions are significantly above the global average. India’s respondents are also the least likely to say that their prospects are worse than those of previous generations of scientists: only 30% do so, compared with 47% globally.

Public-health researcher Suma Nair (left) says that India’s younger generation of scientists might be more optimistic than its senior scientists are, physicist Haroldo Ribeiro (middle) notes that the survey might have picked up on improvements in support for science in Brazil, and economist Sotaro Shibayama says that the competition for young talent is fierce in Japan.Credit: DY Patil Deemed University, Haroldo V. Ribeiro & Sotaro Shibayama, The University of Tokyo

Suma Nair, a public-health researcher at DY Patil University in Mumbai, India, notes that the nation’s science community is multifaceted and complex, and that career satisfaction probably varies considerably across the country. This means that averages can be misleading.

That said, she thinks that India’s young scientists might be behind the strong career optimism recorded. “Those who take up research are probably very passionate about it, with the younger generation especially keen on the start-up culture and innovation,” she says. “They feel that they can make a difference.”

Nair could have a point, because India’s sample has more young respondents than average: 32% self-identify as early-career researchers, compared with 27% globally. Just 14% identify as late career, compared with 20% globally.

Mid-to-late-career scientists might have a less sunny outlook, Nair suggests. Although the Indian government has increased the resources available for young researchers, she says, overall funding levels remain “paltry” compared with leading science nations. “As a senior researcher, I still feel a lot more needs to be done.”

Brazilian resilience

Brazil has the second-highest satisfaction overall (68%). But because the difference with the global average is not statistically significant, this should be interpreted with caution.

“I would for sure not describe Brazilian scientists as the ‘second happiest’ in the world,” says Haroldo Ribeiro, a physicist at the State University of Maringá in Brazil. He says that scientists in his country often complain about their salaries and grant funding, and that both are lower in absolute terms than in wealthier countries.

Rising numbers of Asian and African PhD students choose to study in China

The survey data offer some clues for Brazil’s high satisfaction score. Some 67% of respondents feel satisfied with their job security — significantly more than the global average of 56%. Brazil also has a higher-than-average proportion of full professors — 26% versus 18% globally — even though its distribution of career stages matches the average.

The findings might be explained by the large proportion of survey-takers with permanent positions at public universities or research institutions, notes Bruno de Bezerril Andrade, an infectious-disease researcher at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, who also works in Salvador, Brazil. “Once someone reaches such a position, job security can be substantial,” he says. But the path there is difficult, and most young scientists spend years on fixed-term contracts; many leave science along the way. “There is likely some survivor effect here.”

The country’s researchers also went through a challenging time: grant funding by the government was at a two-decade low in 2021. Ribeiro suspects that the survey could be picking up on the improvements in political support and research funding, including an increase in philanthropy for science. “I would describe the Brazilian scientific community today as more optimistic than comfortable,” he says.

That optimism shines through in the survey data. The proportion of Brazilian scientists who would recommend a science career to students is higher than the world average (72% versus 65%; see ‘Countries differ in career outlooks’).

People in Brazil tend to answer surveys such as this one more positively than do people in many other nations — a subject discussed in depth when Nature reported last year that Brazil’s PhD students were the most satisfied in the world (Nature 646, 1013–1016; 2025). But de Bezerril Andrade does not think the country’s innate optimism explains everything. He calls the optimism of Brazil’s scientists “partly cultural and partly adaptive”. They have had to build meaning and community under unstable conditions, he notes. Such “resilience is admirable in people”, he says. “But it becomes a policy failure when the system depends on it.”

Germany’s pay dividends

Salary satisfaction is higher among Germany’s researchers than for survey participants in any other country with more than 100 respondents. In total, 68% of respondents feel at least somewhat satisfied with their take-home pay compared with 44% globally. Moreover, 22% are ‘extremely satisfied’ with their pay — almost double the global average of 12%.

These findings might be influenced by Germany’s larger sample of scientists working in industry (12%, double the global average), because salaries in industry tend to be higher than academic ones. That Germany is paying scientists well is consistent with data from the Research and Innovation Careers Observatory of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The country tops the index of average gross earnings of employed PhD holders adjusted for purchasing power, coming ahead of Luxembourg, the United States and Switzerland, for instance.

And 87% of respondents can afford some luxuries on top of their basic expenses — significantly more than the 56% who say they can globally. The survey did not define ‘luxuries’, and what counts as a luxury probably differs between countries. But Sauermann says that this aligns with Germany-based scientists feeling secure in their finances. Respondents are also significantly more satisfied than the global average with their access to technologies, their ability to choose hybrid or remote working and their time off. Overall, 67% are satisfied with their work.

However, just 47% of respondents would recommend a career in science, significantly below the global average. Job scarcity might be a factor affecting their advice, especially for academics, says Anne Krüger, a sociologist at the Weizenbaum Institute in Berlin. Many university scientists work part time or have short-term contracts, she says. “That may explain why most researchers would not recommend working in academia.” The survey backs up job precarity being a large drawback of German science careers. When asked what one workplace change would make a big difference, better job security was one of the most common answers from Germany-based scientists, along with better leadership and less bureaucracy.

Although these negative factors might push early-career researchers from Germany towards other professions, the country attracts many scientists from elsewhere. This is reflected in the German sample: 43% of respondents were born outside Germany. By contrast, worldwide, 22% of respondents work outside the country they grew up in. One Greek scientist working at a German university wrote that, apart from its lack of tenure-track positions, the country “is a paradise for research”.

China’s mixed messages

China might be rapidly becoming a science superpower, but it has the lowest proportion (only 51%) of satisfied researchers of all countries with more than 100 respondents. Its scientists are significantly less satisfied with several aspects of their working lives compared with the global average, including with their relationship with colleagues, their time off, their work–life balance and their professional development opportunities.

China-based scientists also have unique career challenges. For instance, 23% of respondents say that the impact of artificial intelligence on their field is one of the biggest challenges they face, significantly above the global average of 12%. They also cite competition for funding and limited language skills as big challenges more often than do scientists from most other countries. However, only 6% consider the effects of geopolitics on science as a main career challenge, significantly below the 16% of respondents who say this globally.

Stagnating salaries present hurdles to career satisfaction

Despite these challenges, most respondents in China are satisfied with their independence (71%) and the meaningfulness of the job (60%) and they feel optimistic about their own prospects (55%). They are also more likely to say that their career prospects are better than those of previous generations of scientists: 37% of respondents from China compared with 31% globally agree with this statement.

Nature’s data on career optimism in countries such as China and India reflect the “changing landscape of science”, says Benedetto Lepori, a research policy specialist at the University of Lugano in Switzerland.

Lepori says that although salaries and funding opportunities in some regions, including India and parts of China, might not match those of Western countries, perceptions of research careers might be more favourable because investment in science is growing in these nations. “Career prospects seem to be mostly related to the perception of working in science systems that are expanding and improving their quality,” he says. For example, in 2023 China spent more research and development funding per researcher than Europe did.

The opposite perception, that science systems are declining, is likely to increase career uncertainty in the United States and in Europe, he notes.

articles.personality_title: Survey reveals what makes scientists happy at work around the world
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
Scientists often face challenges like tight budgets and long hours, but a new global survey shows many still find satisfaction in their work. The 2026 Nature job satisfaction survey collected responses from nearly 4,000 scientists across 133 countries to understand what makes them happy in their jobs.

**What happened**
The survey asked scientists about factors influencing their job satisfaction. It found that meaningful work, good work-life balance, job security, and enough research funding matter more than salary. About 61% of respondents said they were at least moderately satisfied with their jobs, and 65% would recommend a career in research. The survey also compared satisfaction levels across countries like Canada, India, Brazil, Germany, and China.

**Impact**
The findings highlight that money is not the main reason scientists feel happy at work. For example, Canadian scientists reported the highest satisfaction, enjoying good job security, meaningful projects, and remote work options. India’s young scientists showed strong optimism about their careers, while Brazil’s researchers displayed resilience despite funding challenges. Germany’s scientists were most satisfied with their pay but worried about job security. China’s scientists were less satisfied overall but remained hopeful about career prospects. This detailed look helps understand what policies and work environments support scientists’ happiness.

**What’s next step**
These insights can guide governments and institutions to improve science careers by focusing on job security, meaningful work, and flexible work options rather than just salaries. Future surveys will track if these trends continue and how new challenges like artificial intelligence affect scientists’ satisfaction.

**One-sentence takeaway**
Scientists worldwide find job satisfaction mainly through meaningful work and security, with salary playing a smaller role, and this varies by country and career stage.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une enquête révèle ce qui rend les scientifiques heureux au travail dans le monde entier
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte**
Les scientifiques rencontrent souvent des difficultés comme des budgets serrés et de longues heures de travail, mais une nouvelle enquête mondiale montre que beaucoup trouvent tout de même de la satisfaction dans leur métier. L'enquête sur la satisfaction au travail de Nature 2026 a recueilli les réponses de près de 4 000 scientifiques dans 133 pays pour comprendre ce qui les rend heureux dans leur travail.

**Ce qui s'est passé**
L'enquête a interrogé les scientifiques sur les facteurs influençant leur satisfaction professionnelle. Elle a montré que le travail significatif, un bon équilibre entre vie professionnelle et vie privée, la sécurité de l'emploi et un financement suffisant de la recherche comptent plus que le salaire. Environ 61 % des répondants ont déclaré être au moins modérément satisfaits de leur emploi, et 65 % recommanderaient une carrière en recherche. L'enquête a aussi comparé les niveaux de satisfaction dans des pays comme le Canada, l’Inde, le Brésil, l’Allemagne et la Chine.

**Impact**
Les résultats montrent que l'argent n'est pas la principale raison pour laquelle les scientifiques sont heureux au travail. Par exemple, les scientifiques canadiens ont rapporté la plus grande satisfaction, appréciant la sécurité de l'emploi, des projets significatifs et des options de télétravail. Les jeunes scientifiques indiens sont très optimistes quant à leur carrière, tandis que les chercheurs brésiliens font preuve de résilience malgré des difficultés de financement. Les scientifiques allemands sont les plus satisfaits de leur salaire, mais s'inquiètent de la sécurité de l'emploi. Les scientifiques chinois sont moins satisfaits dans l'ensemble, mais restent optimistes quant à leurs perspectives. Cette analyse aide à comprendre quelles politiques et environnements de travail favorisent le bonheur des scientifiques.

**Prochaine étape**
Ces informations peuvent aider les gouvernements et les institutions à améliorer les carrières scientifiques en mettant l'accent sur la sécurité de l'emploi, le travail significatif et les options de travail flexibles plutôt que sur les salaires. Les futures enquêtes suivront si ces tendances se confirment et comment de nouveaux défis comme l'intelligence artificielle influencent la satisfaction des scientifiques.

**Résumé en une phrase**
Dans le monde entier, les scientifiques trouvent principalement leur satisfaction au travail grâce à un travail significatif et à la sécurité, le salaire jouant un rôle moindre, avec des variations selon les pays et les étapes de carrière.
articles.personality_title_es: Una encuesta revela qué hace felices a los científicos en el trabajo en todo el mundo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**
Los científicos a menudo enfrentan desafíos como presupuestos limitados y largas jornadas, pero una nueva encuesta global muestra que muchos aún encuentran satisfacción en su trabajo. La encuesta de satisfacción laboral de Nature 2026 reunió respuestas de casi 4,000 científicos en 133 países para entender qué los hace felices en sus empleos.

**Qué pasó**
La encuesta preguntó a los científicos sobre los factores que influyen en su satisfacción laboral. Encontró que el trabajo significativo, un buen equilibrio entre vida y trabajo, la seguridad laboral y suficiente financiamiento para la investigación son más importantes que el salario. Alrededor del 61% de los encuestados dijeron estar al menos moderadamente satisfechos con sus trabajos, y el 65% recomendaría una carrera en investigación. También comparó los niveles de satisfacción en países como Canadá, India, Brasil, Alemania y China.

**Impacto**
Los resultados muestran que el dinero no es la razón principal por la que los científicos se sienten felices en el trabajo. Por ejemplo, los científicos canadienses reportaron la mayor satisfacción, disfrutando de seguridad laboral, proyectos significativos y opciones de trabajo remoto. Los jóvenes científicos en India mostraron gran optimismo sobre sus carreras, mientras que los investigadores brasileños mostraron resistencia a pesar de los desafíos financieros. Los científicos alemanes estaban más satisfechos con sus sueldos pero preocupados por la seguridad laboral. Los científicos chinos mostraron menor satisfacción general pero permanecen optimistas sobre sus perspectivas. Este análisis ayuda a entender qué políticas y ambientes de trabajo apoyan la felicidad de los científicos.

**Próximo paso**
Estos datos pueden guiar a gobiernos e instituciones para mejorar las carreras científicas enfocándose en la seguridad laboral, el trabajo significativo y opciones flexibles, más que solo en los salarios. Encuestas futuras seguirán estas tendencias y cómo desafíos nuevos como la inteligencia artificial afectan la satisfacción.

**Una frase clave**
Los científicos en todo el mundo encuentran satisfacción laboral principalmente a través de un trabajo significativo y la seguridad, con el salario jugando un papel menor, y esto varía según el país y la etapa de la carrera.
articles.image_prompt: A vibrant, detailed painting of a diverse group of glowing, interconnected laboratory flasks and open books arranged in a circle, each flask emitting softly colored light representing different countries, symbolizing global scientific collaboration and job satisfaction; in the center, a balanced scale made of intertwined DNA strands and research tools, reflecting meaningful work, work–life balance, and optimism in science careers, all rendered in warm, natural earth tones and gentle pastels.
